questions.enonce_markdown:
3. (a) Determine the compounds to be obtained when the schema "$p \cdot \sim q$" replaces "$r$" in the following schemata respectively:

(i) $(q \vee r) \supset (\sim p \cdot q)$

(ii) $(q \vee p) \equiv \sim (r \supset p)$

(iii) Given 'John is sleeping' for 'p'; and 'Mary is cooking' for 'q'; translate the compound obtained in a(i) above into natural language. (2 x 3 marks)

*Alternative For the visually impaired candidates only:*

(i) Explain what is meant by a substitution instance of a propositional form.

(ii) State the truth conditions of a bi-conditional one of whose constituents is a disjunction and the other a negated implication.

(iii) Provide the propositional schema for "the match will end only if the referee so decides". (3 x 2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
A substitution replaces **every occurrence** of $r$ by the whole schema $p \cdot \sim q$, which must be placed in **brackets** so that its scope is kept.

**(i)** $(q \vee r) \supset (\sim p \cdot q)$ becomes

$$[\,q \vee (p \cdot \sim q)\,] \supset (\sim p \cdot q)$$

(there is no $r$ in the consequent, which is unchanged).

**(ii)** $(q \vee p) \equiv \sim (r \supset p)$ becomes

$$(q \vee p) \equiv \sim [\,(p \cdot \sim q) \supset p\,]$$

**(iii) Translation of the compound of (i).** With $p$ = John is sleeping and $q$ = Mary is cooking:

> *If either Mary is cooking, or John is sleeping and Mary is not cooking, then John is not sleeping and Mary is cooking.*

(A truth table shows that this compound has the value of $\sim p$: it is false when $p$ is true and true when $p$ is false, whatever $q$ is.)

| $p$ | $q$ | $q \vee (p \cdot \sim q)$ | $\sim p \cdot q$ | whole compound |
|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|
| T | T | T | F | F |
| T | F | T | F | F |
| F | T | T | T | T |
| F | F | F | F | T |

---

**Alternative for the visually impaired candidates**

**(i) Substitution instance.** A **substitution instance** of a propositional form (schema) is a statement obtained by **replacing each statement variable of the form, uniformly, by a statement** (simple or compound): the same variable is replaced by the same statement at each of its occurrences, and different variables may be replaced by different statements (or by the same one). Example: $(A \cdot B) \supset C$ is a substitution instance of $p \supset q$ (with $p \to A \cdot B$ and $q \to C$).

**(ii) Truth conditions of a biconditional with a disjunction on one side and a negated implication on the other.** Take $(p \vee q) \equiv \sim (r \supset s)$. A biconditional is true exactly when its two constituents have the **same truth value**:

- the disjunction $p \vee q$ is true when at least one of $p$, $q$ is true, and false only when both are false;
- the negated implication $\sim (r \supset s)$ is true only when $r$ is true and $s$ is false, and false otherwise.

So the whole is **true** when (1) at least one of $p$, $q$ is true **and** $r$ is true and $s$ is false, or (2) $p$ and $q$ are both false **and** it is not the case that ($r$ true, $s$ false) (that is, $r$ is false or $s$ is true). It is **false** in all other cases (6 true rows out of 16, checked by program).

**(iii) "The match will end only if the referee so decides."** Let $M$ = the match will end; $D$ = the referee so decides. "Only if" introduces the necessary condition, which is the consequent: $M \supset D$.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(b) Translate the following propositions into predicate logic using universal/ existential quantifiers accordingly:

(i) None-except dogs are animals. (Dx: x is a dog; Ax: x is an animal).

(ii) All but teachers are poor. (Tx: x is a teacher; Px: x is a poor person).

(iii) Certain ladies are beautiful. (Lx: x is a lady; Bx: x is beautiful).

Abraham is a father and Frida is a mother. (Fa: Abraham is a father; Mf: Frida is a mother). (4 x 2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) None except dogs are animals.** "None except dogs are ..." is an exclusive proposition of the type "only dogs are animals": whatever is an animal is a dog.

$$(x)\,(Ax \supset Dx)$$

(equivalently $\sim(\exists x)(Ax \cdot \sim Dx)$: there is no animal that is not a dog.)

**(ii) All but teachers are poor.** This is an exceptive proposition: the non-teachers are poor and (by the force of "but") the teachers are not.

$$(x)\,(\sim Tx \supset Px)\ \cdot\ (x)\,(Tx \supset \sim Px)$$

The first conjunct alone, $(x)(\sim Tx \supset Px)$ ("everything that is not a teacher is poor"), is the minimal translation; the second conjunct expresses the exception ("teachers are not poor"). Together they are equivalent to $(x)(\sim Tx \equiv Px)$.

**(iii) Certain ladies are beautiful.** "Certain" means "at least one": a particular affirmative, with an existential quantifier and a conjunction.

$$(\exists x)\,(Lx \cdot Bx)$$

**(iv) Abraham is a father and Frida is a mother.** Both are **singular** statements about named individuals, so no quantifier is needed:

$$Fa \cdot Mf$$

questions.enonce_markdown:
(c) Test the validity of the following using the short truth table method.

(i) $p \vee (\sim r \cdot q)$
$r \cdot p\ /\ \therefore\ r \vee q$

*Alternative For the visually impaired candidates only:* Explain the principle and the determining factor in the short truth-table technique

(ii) $(C \supset A) \cdot \sim B$
$B \equiv \sim A\ /\ \therefore\ C \cdot B$

*Alternative For the visually impaired candidates only:* Explain the reasoning behind the rules of Conjunction and Addition in Natural deduction (2 x 3 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**The short truth-table method.** To test an argument we try to make the **conclusion false and all the premises true** at once. If this is impossible (the assignment is forced into a contradiction), the argument is **valid**; if a consistent assignment exists, it is a counter-example and the argument is **invalid**.

**(i)** Premises: (1) $p \vee (\sim r \cdot q)$; (2) $r \cdot p$. Conclusion: $r \vee q$.

- Make the conclusion false: a disjunction is false only if both disjuncts are false, so $r = F$ and $q = F$.
- Premise (2), a conjunction, is true only if $r = T$ and $p = T$. But $r = F$ was forced by the conclusion: **contradiction**.

No assignment makes the premises true and the conclusion false, so the argument is **valid**. (A full 8-row truth table gives the same result.)

**(ii)** Premises: (1) $(C \supset A) \cdot \sim B$; (2) $B \equiv \sim A$. Conclusion: $C \cdot B$.

- Premise (1), a conjunction, is true only if $C \supset A$ is true and $\sim B$ is true, so $B = F$.
- With $B = F$ the conclusion $C \cdot B$ is **false** whatever $C$ is: the conclusion is false as required.
- Premise (2): $B \equiv \sim A$ is true when $B$ and $\sim A$ have the same value; $B = F$ forces $\sim A = F$, so $A = T$.
- With $A = T$, $C \supset A$ is true for any $C$.

Consistent assignment: $A = T$, $B = F$, $C = T$ (or $C = F$):

| $A$ | $B$ | $C$ | $(C \supset A)\cdot\sim B$ | $B \equiv \sim A$ | $C \cdot B$ |
|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|
| T | F | T | T | T | **F** |

Both premises are true and the conclusion is false: the argument is **invalid**.

---

**Alternative for the visually impaired candidates**

**Principle and determining factor of the short truth-table technique.** The *principle* is the definition of validity: an argument is invalid if and only if there is **one** assignment of truth values that makes all the premises true and the conclusion false. Instead of writing every row, one searches directly for that row (*reductio*). The *determining factor* is the **truth value of the conclusion and the premises that leave no choice**: one starts by giving the conclusion the value F, then fixes the values forced by it and by the premises that can be true in only one way (a conjunction true, a conditional false), and branches only when no value is forced. If the forced values contradict each other, the argument is valid; if they can all be satisfied, it is invalid.

**Reasoning behind Conjunction and Addition in natural deduction.** Both rules are **truth-preserving**: in no case do they lead from true premises to a false conclusion.

- **Conjunction (Conj.):** from $p$ and, separately, $q$ one may infer $p \cdot q$. If $p$ is true and $q$ is true, the conjunction, which is true exactly when both conjuncts are true, is true.
- **Addition (Add.):** from $p$ one may infer $p \vee q$, for any $q$. A disjunction is true as soon as one disjunct is true; since $p$ is true, $p \vee q$ is true whatever the truth value of the added disjunct $q$.
themes: rules of inference and argument forms

questions.enonce_markdown:
(d) Given A, B, and C as True, X, Y and Z as False, determine the truth-values of the following schemata:

(i) $\sim C \vee (A \cdot \sim Z)$

(ii) $\sim (\sim W \equiv A) \supset (X \vee \sim B)$ (2 x 2.5 marks)

*Alternative For the visually impaired candidates only:*

(i) Explain the meaning of "neither...nor" in terms of the conjunction.

(ii) Describe the reasoning which obtains in rendering the hypothetical statement into a disjunctive. (2 x 2.5 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
Data: $A = B = C = T$; $X = Y = Z = F$.

**(i)** $\sim C \vee (A \cdot \sim Z)$

- $\sim C = \sim T = F$.
- $\sim Z = \sim F = T$, so $A \cdot \sim Z = T \cdot T = T$.
- $F \vee T = T$.

**Answer (i): True.**

**(ii)** $\sim (\sim W \equiv A) \supset (X \vee \sim B)$

- Consequent: $X \vee \sim B = F \vee \sim T = F \vee F = F$.
- Antecedent: since $A = T$, $\sim W \equiv A$ has the value of $\sim W$, so $\sim(\sim W \equiv A)$ has the value of $W$.
- The schema is therefore $W \supset F$, which is equivalent to $\sim W$.

The letter $W$ is **not assigned** by the data. $W$ is the first letter of the series $W, X, Y, Z$ that the examiner treats as false (with $X, Y, Z$); with $W = F$ the antecedent is false and the conditional is **True**. (If $W$ were true, the conditional would be False: its value is exactly $\sim W$.)

**Answer (ii): True** (with $W = F$).

---

**Alternative for the visually impaired candidates**

**(i) "Neither ... nor" in terms of the conjunction.** "Neither $p$ nor $q$" asserts that **both** are false: it is the conjunction of two negations, $\sim p \cdot \sim q$, which is equivalent to the negation of the disjunction, $\sim(p \vee q)$ (De Morgan's law). Example: "Neither John nor Mary came" means "John did not come **and** Mary did not come".

**(ii) Rendering a hypothetical statement into a disjunctive.** The conditional $p \supset q$ is false in only one case: $p$ true and $q$ false. The disjunction $\sim p \vee q$ is false in exactly the same case ($\sim p$ false and $q$ false) and true in the other three, so $p \supset q \equiv \sim p \vee q$ (material implication). "If it rains, the road is wet" can thus be rendered "Either it does not rain or the road is wet". (A 4-row truth table confirms the equivalence.)
